newsitem.title: UK: European bonds nervous, awaiting EMU pact news.
newsitem.headline: European bonds nervous, awaiting EMU pact news.

text.p: European bond markets suffered a bout of nerves on Friday about a detailed stability pact deal for nations planning to join a single euro currency starting in 1999.

European Union finance ministers talked well into the night in Dublin and agreed broad plans to maintain fiscal discipline after the start of economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 but did not set out a final structure.

"It's difficult to say how the cookie will crumble," said Simon Briscoe, chief economist at Nikko in London. "Governments have had a year to discuss this and after 11 hours still couldn't agree on much at all.
"The principle is there but the numbers are not, which is exactly what we've had for a year," he said.

Finance ministers left it to heads of government, meeting for a summit on Friday and Saturday, to settle figures defining "exceptional circumstances" allowing countries to escape fines if they bloated deficits beyond the three percent of gross domestic product level called for in the Maastricht Treaty.
Analysts said the debt markets were likely to remain jittery until a final detailed pact was released.
On Friday, German Bund and French notionnel and Italian BTP bond futures were down by around half a percentage point.
Briscoe said he suspected some form of agreement would be unveiled after the weekend summit but might not have enough in the way of specific numbers to settle bond market nerves.
"The detail may have to be rolled over into the new year and possibly as far as the June EU summit in Amsterdam," he said. "That would leave markets a bit nervous about what's going on."
But others said the broad plans agreed on Thursday should be enough to push a final deal through.
"We are virtually there," said Nigel Richardson, bond economist at Yamaichi International in Europe.
"There may be a couple of things to tie up but come the summit and the final statement, I think we're going to find we've got a stability pact."

Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London, said although noises emerging from Thursday's meeting suggested a more watered down version of the stability pact than Germany had hoped for, the basis was there.
"The outlines from last night are more specific than had originally been set down in the Maastricht Treaty," he said.
"That ought to go some way towards the German side, at the same time as allowing a slightly more liberal interpretation."

Bevan said that from a market perspective, the pact was close enough, saying that even if the finer points of a deal were not hammered out this weekend, bonds would not suffer unduly since the positive sentiment on EMU was behind them.

Yield gaps of high-yield markets such as Spain and Italy versus Germany have tightened sharply. French 10-year yields have been trading largely at parity with their German counterparts for more than six months.

In early European trade, the 10-year BTP/Bund yield gap was broadly steady on Thursday's close at 175 basis points (1.75 percentage point). Spanish bonds, benefiting from a 50 basis point cut in Spain's key money rate to 6.25 percent, narrowed the gap five basis points to 115 from Thursday.
Briscoe, too, noted a wealth of EMU optimism behind the European bond markets but said this might be misplaced.

"The spreads of the non-core contries ought to be a lot wider," he said. "But there has been such a head of steam built up behind these convergence trades, it's hard to see exactly how that is going to be reversed by a fairly bland and on the face of it supportive statement which is what I expect to see later today."
